extracted.intended_audience: trans, nonbinary, and intersex students and families; advocates, policymakers, and members of the public preparing comments on the Title IX athletics rule
extracted.subtask_short: commenting on Title IX athletics rule
extracted.subtask_description: Summary and explanatory guidance on the Department of Education's proposed Title IX athletics rule, including the legal test schools must meet to limit or deny a student's eligibility to participate on teams consistent with their gender identity. Useful for advocates, affected students/families, and commenters preparing notice-and-comment input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-sport/level/grade application
rubrics_metrics.description: If a recipient adopts or applies sex-related criteria that would limit or deny a student’s eligibility to participate on a male or female team consistent with their gender identity, such criteria must, for each sport, level of competition, and grade or education level: ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule requires any limitation be evaluated separately for each sport, level of competition, and grade/education level rather than applied categorically across all sports or ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantially related to an important educational objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Such criteria must ... (i) be substantially related to the achievement of an important educational objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first prong of the proposed test and echoes intermediate scrutiny: the school must identify an important educational objective and show the restriction is substantially related to achieving it. The Department ties this to Equal Protection analysis and prior Department standards for single-sex classes/extracurriculars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize harms to affected students
rubrics_metrics.description: Such criteria must ... (ii) minimize harms to students whose opportunity to participate on a male or female team consistent with their gender identity would be limited or denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any restriction must be the least harmful means practicable; schools must consider and prefer less harmful alternatives and cannot adopt criteria that inflict unnecessary harm on trans, nonbinary, or intersex students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on categorical bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit schools from categorically banning trans students from participating in sports consistent with their gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If finalized as interpreted here, state laws that impose blanket bans (the brief cites 21 states with blanket bans) would violate Title IX. The rule would effectively bar broad, across-the-board exclusions at elementary, middle, and (in most cases) high school levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited justifications: transphobia, intent to harm, exclusion, stereotypes, administrative convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools could not justify an exclusion of trans students from playing sports based on disapproval of trans students, a desire to harm a particular student, a desire to exclude trans students from sports, adherence to sex stereotypes, or for administrative convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explicitly lists these rationales as impermissible. A valid justification must reflect an important educational objective rather than discriminatory motives or mere convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited reliance on overbroad generalizations or false assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools could also not justify an exclusion of trans students based on overbroad generalizations or false assumptions, such as restrictions that assume categorical superiority or physical advantages for trans athletes across all sports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: schools would not be able to assume that trans women and girls have the same physical abilities as cisgender boys and men. Blanket assertions of advantage across all sports are disallowed; any factual claims must be sport- and circumstance-specific and evidence-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to evaluate harm and consider less-harmful alternatives (documentation/privacy example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require schools to evaluate the harm that any restriction would have on an affected student. If there is any less harmful alternative, the school would not be permitted to adopt the more harmful criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a school requires a student to provide documentation of their gender identity, the school must minimize potential harms (e.g., difficulty obtaining documentation, risk of invasion of privacy or disclosure of confidential information) and consider alternatives before imposing that requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with Equal Protection intermediate scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed test is similar to the analysis for determining whether ... 'sex-based classifications' violate the Equal Protection Clause: that they serve important governmental objectives and are substantially related to achievement of those objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes courts have applied this test to state sports bans; the rule is presented as consistent with constitutional intermediate scrutiny and with Department standards already applied to K–12 single-sex classes and activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule does not mandate limiting participation
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not require that schools limit trans students’ participation in athletics in any way: the 15 states (including DC) that currently allow trans students to participate in K-12 sports consistent with gender identity would be in compliance with the Title IX athletics rule as proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is framed to permit inclusion and does not force schools to adopt restrictions — only to ensure any restriction meets the two-prong test and harm-minimization requirement. The page emphasizes that inclusive policies 'harm no one.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural status: proposed rule and comment period
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a proposed rule that the public will be able to weigh in on during the 30-day comment period (until May 15, 2023), and it is possible the Department will make changes and revisions to the text before finalizing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: stakeholders should submit comments during the notice-and-comment period and continue advocacy at state and local levels since the rule is not yet final and state laws may still be enacted or enforced in the meantime.
